MEXICO CITY (AP) — Powerful Hurricane Polo sent bands of heavy rain across Mexico’s Pacific coast early Thursday as a growing Tropical Storm Nolo approached Hawaii with the potential for catastrophic flooding.

Polo was forecast to maintain Category 5 strength as it skirts Mexico’s coast over the next few days. Rain and strong winds had already started to pummel the coast, with waves crashing onto the normally pristine beaches.
While the eye and the strongest winds were expected to remain at sea, the heavy rains could cause life-threatening flooding and landslides, according to the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami.

[![This photo provided by NOAA shows Hurricane Polo strengthening in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Mexico on Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026. (NOAA via AP)](https://www.winnipegfreepress.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/6ab2c674d98934d156a5c7e9jpeg.jpg?w=1000)](https://www.winnipegfreepress.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/6ab2c674d98934d156a5c7e9jpeg.jpg?w=1000)
This photo provided by NOAA shows Hurricane Polo strengthening in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Mexico on Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026. (NOAA via AP)

Farther west in the Pacific, Tropical Storm Nolo was churning about 295 miles (475 kilometers) south of South Point, Hawaii. It was forecast to become a hurricane by Thursday night and was expected to approach the Big Island as early as Friday. A hurricane watch was issued for Hawaii County.

Gov. Josh Green’s office said public schools and state and county offices on the Big Island will close Thursday and Friday, while Maui County will shutter them on Friday ahead of the threat of heavy rain, winds and flooding. Forecasters said the storm could drop up to 20 inches (51 centimeters) of rain.
**Polo could bring flooding and mudslides to Mexico’s Pacific coast**

Concepción López Villegas was busily bolstering her seaside restaurant in Lázaro Cárdenas, Michoacán state, against the expected onslaught of rain. Strong waves were already hitting some beaches and López Villegas said she feared the storm could destroy the small business she worked decades to build.
“We’re worried and trying to protect our businesses,” López Villegas said. “And of course, we’re sad because it’s our heritage, our legacy that from one moment to another could be destroyed.”
Guerrero state was particularly at risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides, the hurricane center said.
Polo was swirling about 130 miles (209 kilometers) south-southwest of Zihuatanejo early Thursday and was moving northwest

**ABOUT REGENCY SILVER CORP.**

Regency Silver Corp. (TSXV: RSMX) (OTCQB: RSMXF) (FSE: ZJ90) is a Canadian mineral exploration company focused on high-grade gold, silver, and copper in Mexico. The Company’s flagship asset is the **Dios Padre Project in Yecora, Sonora, Mexico**, where Regency Silver has discovered a large, high-grade gold-copper-silver system interpreted as a magmatic-hydrothermal breccia that widens with depth.

Regency recently announced an agreement to acquire the past producing La Dura gold mine only 20 km from Dios Padre and 6 km from the Mulatos mine.

## Pollinator Park volunteers place giant monarch art installation
![Gallery image](https://ogden_images.s3.amazonaws.com/www.nujournal.com/images/2026/09/23190406/Group2-1100x733.webp)

The volunteer who created the Pollinator Park’s new monarch sculpture stand alongside it shortly after it was placed in the park on Tuesday. In photo: Kay Martin (left), Joe Gartner (back), Julie Gartner (front) and Deb Steinberg (right). Photo by Clay Schuldt
![Gallery image](https://ogden_images.s3.amazonaws.com/www.nujournal.com/images/2026/09/23190422/sculpt-637x840.webp)
The eight-foot-wide wooden monarch sculpture was placed in the New Ulm’s Pollinator Park Tuesday. The sculpture will remain in the park through autumn. Photo by Clay Schuldt
![Gallery image](https://ogden_images.s3.amazonaws.com/www.nujournal.com/images/2026/09/23190414/Joe3-1100x733.webp)

Pollinator Park volunteer Joe Gartner said took roughly 40 hours for him to draw the outline for the park’s new monarch sculpture. It took another couple weeks for volunteers to paint it. Photo by Clay Schuldt
![Gallery image](https://ogden_images.s3.amazonaws.com/www.nujournal.com/images/2026/09/23190359/DSC_0837-1100x733.webp)

The Pollinator Park monarch sculpture is the first step in a larger art installation plan. The idea is to eventually have a sculpture representing all four stages of the monarch lifecycle in the park. Volunteers began with single wooden sculpture as a low-cost way to start. Photo by Clay Schuldt
NEW ULM - No, that is not Mothra in New Ulm's Pollinator Park. It is actually a new wooden sculpture created by park volunteers.
The eight-foot-wide monarch sculpture was put in place Tuesday evening by volunteers.
"It is a low-cost way of adding some new art to the park," volunteer Deb Steinberg said.
Fellow volunteer Joe Gartner purchased the wood for the project and traced the outline for the monarch using a projector. He said it took roughly 40 hours to outline the sculpture.
It took another few weeks for Steinberg, Kay Martin and Julie Gartner to fully paint the massive monarch.
Actually placing the monarch in the park took another six hours. Joe Gartner said he and Bob Beck struggled to get the posts in the ground as the area was relatively rocky.
The monarch sculpture has been on the wish list for Pollinator Park volunteers for a few years, but this is only the first step.

Steinberg said they hope to add other sculptures that show the entire lifecycle of the monarch, starting with the caterpillar stage. In addition, the wooden monarch sculpture is only a temporary installation.
Joe Gartner said he was not sure the wooden monarch sculpture would hold up through winter. They plan to take it down before the snow buries it. It can go up again in the spring.
Steinberg said eventually they hope to have metal sculptures on the site that can remain up year-round, but they are still raising money for the permanent sculpture.
For now, the park volunteers hope to have the wooden sculpture up during the monarch season.
Steinberg said there are still some monarchs in the New Ulm area, but the majority have already left for Mexico.
The monarch sculpture will remain up for at least the next several weeks. Pollinator Park volunteers hope it will attract visitors to the park to explore and take photos.

Steinberg said if a person stand in the right place during a photo it will look like they have butterfly wings. There is a wood post with a phone stand about six-feet from the sculpture to help visitor take the perfect selfie.
"It will look like people are ready to take flight," she said.

> 📍 **階層**: Home > Hispanic Heritage Month On 82nd Street
on September 24, 2026
Every year from September 15 to October 15, the country observes Hispanic Heritage Month, a time to celebrate the history, culture, and contributions of Hispanic and Latino Americans.

Why September 15? This date marks the independence anniversary of five Central American nations Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, and Nicaragua, all of which gained independence on the same day in 1821. Mexico celebrates its independence just one day later, on September 16, and Chile on September 18, making this stretch of the calendar a natural moment for celebration across the region.

Why it matters here on 82nd Street? Jackson Heights & Elmhurst are one of the most vibrant Latino communities in New York City and that spirit lives in our restaurants, our shops, our art, and the people who’ve built their lives and businesses here. This month, the 82nd Street Partnership is celebrating that legacy the best way we know how: by shining a light on our own community.
